Furthermore, NSAIDs can competitively block aspirin from accessing its target acetylation site on COX-1, thereby blunting the irreversible cardioprotective antiplatelet effect of aspirin 8 9 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: For a patient on chronic systemic glucocorticoid therapy undergoing major abdominal or cardiac surgery, what perioperative stress-dose steroid regimen is indicated?
options: Continue home dose only without supplemental steroids
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction, followed by 200 mg over 24 hours (infusion), then double the usual home oral dose for 24–48 hours once taking oral meds
Dexamethasone 40 mg IV push every 6 hours for 5 days
Stop all steroids 24 hours prior to surgery to ensure wound healing
questions.explanation: Major surgical stress requires perioperative hydrocortisone coverage to prevent acute adrenal crisis: 100 mg IV at induction, followed by a continuous IV infusion of 200 mg over 24 hours. Once the patient resumes oral intake, double their usual home dose for 24–48 hours before returning to baseline maintenance 29 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: In adult patients, what single ingested dose of paracetamol is recognized to cause hepatotoxicity, and what dose is considered potentially fatal?
options: Hepatotoxicity at 4 g; fatal at 8 g
Hepatotoxicity at 10–15 g; fatal at 20–25 g or more
Hepatotoxicity at 20 g; fatal at 40 g
Hepatotoxicity at 5 g; fatal at 10 g
questions.explanation: The maximum recommended adult oral dose of paracetamol is 4 g/day (500 mg–1 g every 4–6 hours) 5 . Hepatotoxicity can occur after a single acute ingestion of 10–15 g, whereas single doses of 20–25 g or more are potentially fatal 6 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Local anesthetics (such as lidocaine, bupivacaine, and ropivacaine) produce nerve blockades by targeting which cellular channel?
questions.explanation: Local anesthetics act as sodium channel blockers to inhibit nerve impulse conduction during local and regional nerve blockades 17 18 . Concurrent use with Class I antiarrhythmics (quinidine) or prior amiodarone use are noted contraindications 18 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What classic clinical triad defines acute opioid toxicity (morphine overdose)?
options: Coma, respiratory depression, and pinpoint pupils
questions.explanation: Acute opioid toxicity presents with the classic clinical triad of coma, respiratory depression, and pinpoint (miotic) pupils 14 15 . Definitive treatment includes supportive ventilation and the administration of naloxone 15 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the distinct biochemical mechanism of action of paracetamol (acetaminophen) compared to classic NSAIDs?
options: Irreversible acetylation of peripheral COX-1 enzymes
Competitive antagonism of central NMDA receptors
Nonselective COX inhibition acting at the peroxide site of the enzyme
Direct activation of GABA-A receptors in the spinal cord
questions.explanation: Paracetamol is a nonselective COX inhibitor that acts uniquely at the peroxide site of the cyclooxygenase enzyme 4 . High concentrations of peroxides present at sites of tissue inflammation reduce its COX-inhibitory activity, which explains why paracetamol exhibits strong analgesic and antipyretic effects but only weak anti-inflammatory activity 5 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the mechanism of action and maximum daily dose of methoxyflurane when used for emergency analgesia?
options: GABA receptor agonist; maximum daily dose of 6 ml (2 handheld inhalers)
Sodium channel blocker; maximum 12 ml daily
questions.explanation: Methoxyflurane acts as a GABA receptor agonist 16 . It is administered via a 3 ml handheld inhaler, with a maximum daily dose of 6 ml (2 inhalers) 16 . High anesthetic doses carry risks of hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity 16 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary cellular mechanism by which glucocorticoids exert their potent anti-inflammatory effects?
options: Direct blockade of histamine H1 receptors
Selective inhibition of COX-3 in the central nervous system
questions.explanation: Glucocorticoids inhibit phospholipase A2, suppressing the release of arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids and thereby blocking downstream synthesis of both leukotrienes and prostaglandins 27 28 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the recommended starting dose and titration schedule for pregabalin in the management of chronic neuropathic pain?
options: Start 300 mg once daily at bedtime; increase to 300 mg TID after 2 days
Start 75 mg twice daily; increase to 150 mg twice daily (300 mg/day total) after 1 week
Start 150 mg twice daily; increase to 600 mg/day after 3 days
Start 50 mg three times daily; increase to 100 mg TID after 1 month
questions.explanation: Pregabalin for chronic neuropathic pain is started at 75 mg twice daily and may be titrated after 1 week to 150 mg twice daily (300 mg/day total) based on patient response 25 . Gabapentin starts at 300 mg once daily at bedtime (Days 1–2), building to 300 mg TID by Days 5–7 25 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What single intravenous dose of dexamethasone is recommended at anesthesia induction for the prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV)?
questions.explanation: A single IV dose of 4 to 8 mg dexamethasone in adults is commonly administered at the induction of anesthesia to prevent postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) and reduce postoperative edema 29 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: When managing acute pain in emergency settings, what essential rule governs analgesic dose escalation for patients experiencing severe pain?
options: Always double the initial dose of the currently administered NSAID
Ensure any newly added analgesic drug belongs to a different pharmacological class
questions.explanation: Guidelines for managing acute pain in emergency settings mandate that when stepping up therapy for moderate or severe pain, additional analgesic options must be of a different pharmacological class 19 more_horiz . Administering a second different NSAID to a patient already receiving an NSAID is strictly contraindicated 21 22 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which drug-drug interaction warning specifically applies to the concurrent use of pregabalin and gabapentin?
options: Multiplies side effects dramatically without providing additional pain relief
questions.explanation: Combining pregabalin and gabapentin together dramatically multiplies adverse side effects (such as dizziness and drowsiness) without increasing therapeutic pain relief 26 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a primary contraindication to the administration of ketamine for acute analgesia?
questions.explanation: Ketamine is a glutamate/NMDA receptor antagonist that causes cardiac stimulation (increase in heart rate and blood pressure) 15 . It is strictly contraindicated in patients with eclampsia or pre-eclampsia, uncontrolled hypertension, and severe cardiac disease 15 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which pain assessment tool is specifically validated for evaluating pain in sedated or mechanically ventilated unconscious surgical patients?
questions.explanation: The Behavioral Pain Scale (BPS) evaluates pain in sedated or unconscious patients using three parameters: facial expression, upper limb movement, and compliance with mechanical ventilation 2 . The FLACC scale is used for pediatric patients aged 2 months to 7 years 3 , while Wong-Baker FACES is used for pediatric or cognitively impaired patients 2 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which peripheral pharmacological action is directly produced by morphine administration?
options: Diarrhea due to accelerated fecal mass transit
Urinary retention due to increased bladder and sphincter tone
Uterine hyper-stimulation causing rapid precipitous labor
questions.explanation: Morphine produces peripheral actions including vagal stimulation (bradycardia), histamine release (hypotension and pruritus), constipation (delayed fecal mass transit and increased water absorption), biliary colic (biliary smooth muscle contraction), and urinary retention (increased bladder and sphincter tone) 11 12 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Why are conventional NSAIDs generally ineffective against pain originating from hollow viscera, with the primary clinical exception of primary dysmenorrhea?
options: Visceral smooth muscle lacks COX-1 and COX-2 receptors
NSAIDs cannot penetrate visceral peritoneal membranes
Primary dysmenorrhea cramps are specifically driven by endometrial prostaglandin release
Visceral pain is exclusively mediated by central mu-opioid pathways
questions.explanation: NSAIDs are effective against low-to-moderate inflammatory somatic pain (such as arthritic and postoperative pain) but are less effective against hollow visceral pain 7 . Primary dysmenorrhea is a major exception because uterine cramps and associated symptoms are directly caused by the local release of prostaglandins by the endometrium during menstruation 7 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Why is head trauma listed as a key contraindication for morphine administration?
options: Morphine induces central respiratory depression and carbon dioxide retention, elevating intracranial pressure (ICP)
Morphine causes acute seizure activity in head-injured patients
questions.explanation: Morphine is contraindicated in head trauma because respiratory depression leads to hypercapnia (CO2 retention), which induces cerebral vasodilation and increases intracranial pressure (ICP) 12 13 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: A 58‑year‑old man with a history of chronic pancreatitis presents with an acute episode of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. He is started on intravenous morphine for pain control. Which of the following statements about morphine’s pharmacodynamics in this patient is most accurate?
options: Morphine’s analgesic effect is primarily mediated by activation of μ‑opioid receptors in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, leading to decreased release of substance P and glutamate.
Morphine is metabolised by CYP2D6 into morphine‑6‑glucuronide, which is the main active metabolite responsible for analgesia.
Morphine’s analgesic effect is enhanced by co‑administration of ketamine due to synergistic NMDA receptor blockade.
Morphine’s analgesic effect is primarily mediated by activation of κ‑opioid receptors in the peripheral nervous system, reducing peripheral nociceptor firing.
questions.explanation: Morphine exerts its analgesic effect mainly through μ‑opioid receptor activation in the dorsal horn, inhibiting neurotransmitter release. The other options describe incorrect receptor targets or metabolic pathways. Morphine is metabolised to morphine‑3‑glucuronide (inactive) and morphine‑6‑glucuronide (active) but the primary analgesic effect is via μ‑receptors, not CYP2D6. Ketamine’s NMDA blockade does not synergise with morphine for analgesia, and κ‑receptors are not the main site of action.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which of the following drugs is most commonly used as a first‑line agent to treat acute peptic ulcer bleeding by reducing gastric acid secretion?
questions.explanation: Omeprazole, a proton‑pump inhibitor, is the preferred first‑line therapy for acute peptic ulcer bleeding because it provides the most potent and sustained suppression of gastric acid secretion, promoting ulcer healing. H2‑receptor antagonists also reduce acid but are less effective than PPIs. Metoclopramide and sucralfate are used for other indications (motility and ulcer coating, respectively).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: A 65‑year‑old patient with a history of hypertension is started on a new antihypertensive drug. He reports a persistent dry cough. Which class of medication is most likely responsible for this side effect?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II and also inhibit breakdown of bradykinin, leading to a dry cough. Beta‑blockers, calcium channel blockers and diuretics are not associated with this adverse effect.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: According to preoperative holding protocols, how many days before elective surgery must oral Warfarin be held, and how many hours before surgery must therapeutic Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH) be stopped?
options: Warfarin held 2 days before; LMWH held 6 hours before
Warfarin held 5 days before; LMWH held 24 hours before
Warfarin held 7 days before; LMWH held 48 hours before
Warfarin held 1 day before; LMWH held 12 hours before
questions.explanation: Elective surgery guidelines specify holding oral Warfarin 5 days before surgery. Therapeutic LMWH must be stopped 24 hours before surgery (prophylactic LMWH is held 12 hours before; IV unfractionated heparin is held 4–6 hours before).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Hemorrhagic cystitis (hematuria) is a classic adverse effect of Cyclophosphamide caused by acrolein accumulation. Which agent is administered to prevent or manage this complication?
questions.explanation: Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating prodrug metabolized into phosphoramide mustard (active cytotoxic agent) and acrolein (toxic metabolite causing hemorrhagic cystitis). It is managed with aggressive fluid intake, MESNA, or N-acetylcysteine.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: In a patient receiving therapeutic unfractionated heparin (UFH), what is the target activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT) therapeutic range relative to baseline?
questions.explanation: Normal aPTT is 25–33 seconds. In heparin toxicity or over-anticoagulation, target controlled aPTT (CaPTT) is maintained at 2 to 3 times the normal baseline value.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Match the cytotoxic antibiotic to its pathognomonic organ-specific toxicity: Doxorubicin | Bleomycin | Mitomycin
options: Doxorubicin = Pulmonary fibrosis; Bleomycin = Nephrotoxicity; Mitomycin = Cardiotoxicity
Doxorubicin = Cardiotoxicity; Bleomycin = Pneumonitis & Pulmonary Fibrosis; Mitomycin = Nephrotoxicity
Doxorubicin = Ototoxicity; Bleomycin = Cardiotoxicity; Mitomycin = Hepatotoxicity
Doxorubicin = Nephrotoxicity; Bleomycin = Neurotoxicity; Mitomycin = Cardiotoxicity
questions.explanation: Cytotoxic antibiotics exhibit distinct organ toxicities: Doxorubicin causes cardiotoxicity; Bleomycin causes pneumonitis and pulmonary fibrosis; Mitomycin causes nephrotoxicity.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Regarding cancer chemotherapy during pregnancy, during which gestational period is cytotoxic chemotherapy strictly an absolute classic contraindication?
questions.explanation: Cytotoxic chemotherapy is strictly avoided during the 1st Trimester (organogenesis stage) due to high teratogenic risk. Methotrexate is highlighted as an absolute classic contraindication.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: To prevent ibuprofen from interfering with the antiplatelet cardioprotective effect of low-dose aspirin, what administration timing rule must be followed?
options: Take aspirin simultaneously with ibuprofen at mealtime
Take aspirin at least 1 hour before or at least 8 hours after ibuprofen
Take ibuprofen strictly 30 minutes before aspirin
Double the dose of ibuprofen when taking aspirin
questions.explanation: Ibuprofen reversibly binds COX-1 and competitively prevents aspirin from reaching its target acetylation site. Therefore, aspirin should be ingested at least 1 hour before or at least 8 hours after ibuprofen.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the mechanism of action and clinical contraindication of Tranexamic Acid (TXA) in bleeding management?
options: Direct factor VIIa activator; contraindicated in severe liver disease
Lysine analogue blocking plasminogen/plasmin lysine-binding sites; contraindicated in renal disease
Vitamin K epoxide reductase activator; contraindicated in hypertension
Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa antagonist; contraindicated in heart failure
questions.explanation: Tranexamic acid (and EACA) is a synthetic lysine analogue that blocks the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen and plasmin, preventing plasmin-mediated fibrin degradation. It is contraindicated in renal disease.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the precise biochemical mechanism of action of unfractionated heparin (UFH)?
options: Direct competitive inhibition of the thrombin catalytic site
Binding to antithrombin III to accelerate inactivation of factors IIa, IXa, Xa, XIa, and XIIa
Inhibition of hepatic vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1)
questions.explanation: Unfractionated heparin acts indirectly by binding to antithrombin III, which markedly accelerates the inactivation of clotting factors IIa (thrombin), IXa, Xa, XIa, and XIIa.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What percentage of human cancers reactivate the reverse transcriptase enzyme telomerase to bypass cellular senescence and achieve immortality?
questions.explanation: Telomeres consist of repetitive TTAGGG DNA end-cap sequences. Approximately 90% of human cancers reactivate telomerase (a reverse transcriptase enzyme), preventing telomere shortening and conferring cellular immortality.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What pharmacological rationale explains why low-dose aspirin (60–325 mg daily) remains uniquely effective as an antiplatelet agent compared to non-selective NSAIDs like ibuprofen?
options: Aspirin reversibly blocks ADP P2Y12 receptors on vascular endothelium
Mature platelets are anucleate and cannot synthesize new COX-1 enzymes following irreversible acetylation by aspirin
Aspirin selectively inhibits COX-2 in mature circulating platelets
Ibuprofen permanently destroys hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes
questions.explanation: Aspirin selectively and irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1 (100 times more potent than against COX-2). Because circulating platelets lack nuclei, they cannot synthesize new COX-1 protein, resulting in permanent enzyme inhibition for the remainder of the platelet lifespan (7–10 days). Non-selective NSAIDs (like ibuprofen) inhibit COX-1 reversibly and lack persistent antithrombotic effects.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: When transfusing Cryoprecipitate to an Rh-negative (Rh -ve) pregnant patient, what special blood banking directive must be strictly observed?
options: Cryoprecipitate must be infused over a minimum of 24 hours
Cryoprecipitate must be co-administered with high-dose aspirin
Cryoprecipitate must be reconstituted with 5% Dextrose
questions.explanation: Cryoprecipitate is a concentrated plasma protein fraction containing Factor VIII, vWF, and fibrinogen. When administered to Rh-negative (Rh -ve) pregnant women, Cryoprecipitate must be strictly Rh-negative to avoid Rh isoimmunization.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which antimetabolite anticancer agent acts as a folic acid antagonist, and what specific rescue drug is administered on non-treatment days to mitigate severe mucosal and hematologic toxicity?
questions.explanation: Methotrexate is a folic acid antagonist antimetabolite. To prevent lethal normal tissue toxicity (megaloblastic anemia, mucosal ulceration, hepatotoxicity), Folinic Acid (Leucovorin) rescue is administered on non-methotrexate days.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which antiplatelet drug is an oral phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibitor approved specifically for symptomatic management of intermittent claudication, but strictly contraindicated in heart failure (CHF)?
questions.explanation: Cilostazol is an oral PDE inhibitor that increases cAMP, causing vasodilation and antiplatelet activity. It is indicated for intermittent claudication in peripheral arterial disease, but is strictly contraindicated in patients with Congestive Heart Failure (CHF). Dipyridamole causes the "coronary steal phenomenon" in clinically unstable angina.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which coagulation factor deficiency specifically defines Hemophilia B (Christmas disease)?
questions.explanation: Factor VIII deficiency causes Hemophilia A (classic hemophilia), whereas Factor IX (Christmas factor) deficiency causes Hemophilia B (Christmas disease). Factor XI deficiency is termed Plasma Thromboplastin Antecedent (PTA) deficiency.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which condition is listed as an ABSOLUTE contraindication to thrombolytic/fibrinolytic therapy?
options: Ischemic stroke within the preceding 3 months
questions.explanation: Absolute contraindications to thrombolytics include: severe intracranial hemorrhage, structural cerebral vascular lesions, retinal hemorrhage, malignant intracranial neoplasms, ischemic stroke within 3 months, active bleeding ( excluding menses ), and significant closed-head or facial trauma/surgery within 3 months.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) functions as a direct thrombin inhibitor and has a specific FDA-approved monoclonal antibody reversal agent (Idarucizumab)?
questions.explanation: Dabigatran is an oral direct thrombin (Factor IIa) inhibitor with predictable pharmacokinetics that requires no routine monitoring. Its anticoagulant activity can be rapidly and completely reversed by the specific monoclonal antibody Idarucizumab. Rivaroxaban inhibits Factor Xa (reversed by Andexanet alfa).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which feature correctly distinguishes Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH, e.g., enoxaparin) from Unfractionated Heparin (UFH)?
options: LMWH requires routine daily aPTT monitoring
LMWH has lower oral bioavailability and a shorter half-life than UFH
LMWH is excreted renally and its neutralization by protamine sulfate is only partial
LMWH carries a higher risk of Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (>5%)
questions.explanation: LMWH has high subcutaneous bioavailability (90%), a longer half-life (4 hours), is eliminated via renal excretion, carries a lower risk of HIT (<1%), and requires no routine monitoring. Crucially, protamine sulfate provides complete neutralization for UFH, but only partial neutralization for LMWH (enoxaparin).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which fibrinolytic agent is a recombinant human tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA) characterized by a long half-life that allows it to be administered as a single IV BOLUS?
questions.explanation: Fibrin-specific thrombolytic agents include Alteplase and Tenecteplase (recombinant human tPAs). Tenecteplase has a prolonged half-life (t½), enabling rapid administration as a single IV bolus. Streptokinase and Urokinase are non-fibrin-specific agents.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Why can warfarin administration paradoxically precipitate acute skin necrosis early during the initiation of therapy?
options: Warfarin causes direct non-immunologic necrosis of vascular smooth muscle cells
Warfarin inhibits endogenous anticoagulant Protein C and Protein S faster than clotting factors II, IX, and X
Warfarin induces rapid local histamine release and mast cell degranulation
Warfarin triggers acute immune complex deposition in dermal capillaries
questions.explanation: Warfarin inhibits the gamma-carboxylation of Vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) and anticoagulant proteins (Protein C and Protein S). Because Protein C has a shorter half-life than factors II, IX, and X, its levels drop first, resulting in a transient hypercoagulable state and microvascular thrombosis (skin necrosis) before full anticoagulation is achieved.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Why is the subcutaneous (SC) route of Vitamin K1 (Phytonadione) administration clinically avoided, and what life-threatening risk is associated with rapid IV push of Vitamin K1?
options: SC causes immediate skin necrosis; rapid IV causes renal failure
SC shows an erratic absorption pattern; rapid IV causes severe dyspnea, chest/back pain, flushing, and death
SC precipitates deep vein thrombosis; rapid IV causes severe hypoglycemia
SC causes osteotoxicity; rapid IV causes acute red man syndrome
questions.explanation: Subcutaneous administration of Vitamin K1 is avoided because of an erratic absorption pattern. Rapid IV push of Vitamin K1 can trigger severe anaphylactoid infusion reactions presenting with dyspnea, chest and back pain, flushing, vascular collapse, and death.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Bulk-forming laxatives (such as Psyllium and Methylcellulose) are strictly contraindicated in which clinical scenario?
options: Patients with obstructive symptoms and megacolon
Patients with mild hemorrhoids and painful defecation
Chronic management of irritable bowel syndrome
questions.explanation: Bulk-forming agents require functional bowel motility and open lumen; they are contraindicated in bowel obstruction and megacolon.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Prucalopride is classified under which pharmacological category for treating chronic constipation?
options: High-affinity 5-HT4 receptor agonist acting as a prokinetic agent
questions.explanation: Prucalopride is a selective 5-HT4 agonist that enhances GI motility and is approved for chronic constipation.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Under what clinical circumstance are antidiarrheal drugs strictly contraindicated and must be avoided?
options: Chronic diarrhea associated with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
Mild to moderate acute watery diarrhea
Patients presenting with bloody diarrhea, high fever, or systemic toxicity
questions.explanation: Antidiarrheals must be avoided in bloody diarrhea, high fever, or systemic toxicity due to the risk of worsening the underlying condition (e.g., bacterial invasion).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What critical conditions must be actively excluded prior to administering Loperamide for the management of postoperative diarrhea?
options: Mild postoperative nausea and electrolyte imbalances
Bowel obstruction, ileus, anastomotic leak, and infectious causes (especially Clostridioides difficile)
Hyperactive bowel sounds and mild incisional pain
questions.explanation: Using loperamide in the presence of obstruction, ileus, anastomotic leak, or C. difficile can precipitate toxic megacolon or worsen sepsis.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is a classic pathological finding associated with long-term chronic use of anthraquinone stimulant laxatives (like Senna and Cascara sagrada)?
options: Severe melanosis coli (brown pigmentation of the colon)
Complete destruction of gastric parietal cells
Hypertrophic muscular layer resembling Hirschsprung disease
questions.explanation: Chronic use of anthraquinones causes characteristic brown pigmentation of the colonic mucosa known as melanosis coli.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is a critical drug interaction concern when administering NK1 receptor blockers (like aprepitant) alongside certain chemotherapeutic agents or other medications?
options: They induce CYP2E1, causing rapid clearance of opioids
They inhibit the CYP3A4 hepatic metabolic pathway, which can lead to toxic accumulation of drugs like docetaxel, paclitaxel, and vincristine
They completely block renal tubular secretion of platinum compounds
They displace plasma proteins, triggering sudden fatal kernicterus
questions.explanation: NK1 receptor blockers inhibit CYP3A4, potentially increasing plasma concentrations and toxicity of chemotherapy agents metabolized by this pathway.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is a major clinical use of Octreotide, a synthetic analog of somatostatin?
options: Emergency management of acute opioid overdose
Treatment of diarrhea induced by neuroendocrine tumors of the GI tract and short bowel syndrome
First-line eradication therapy for Helicobacter pylori infection
questions.explanation: Octreotide inhibits hormone secretion and fluid loss, making it useful in neuroendocrine tumor-induced diarrhea and short bowel syndrome.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary clinical indication and mechanism of Bile Salt Binding-Resins (such as Cholestyramine) in gastrointestinal disorders?
options: They bind unabsorbed bile salts in patients with terminal ileum disease or resection, decreasing secretory diarrhea
They neutralize gastric acid and coat gastric ulcers to prevent perforation
They stimulate colonic water secretion to treat severe refractory constipation
They inhibit pancreatic lipase enzymes to treat fat malabsorption
questions.explanation: Terminal ileum disease causes bile salt malabsorption leading to diarrhea; binding resins like cholestyramine effectively treat this condition.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary mechanism of action of Stool-wetting agents (Surfactants) such as Docusate sodium?
options: Irreversibly paralyzing the myenteric plexus to stop painful spasms
Allowing mixing of aqueous and fatty substances to soften the stool and stimulating fluid/electrolyte secretion
Coating the entire colonic mucosa with an impermeable resin layer
Releasing carbon dioxide gas to mechanically fragment hard fecaliths
questions.explanation: Docusate acts as a surfactant allowing water and fats to mix into the stool while stimulating fluid secretion.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary peripheral mechanism of action through which 5-HT3 receptor antagonists (such as Ondansetron and Tropisetron) exert their potent antiemetic effect?
options: Inhibition of central histamine H1 receptors in the vestibular nuclei
Blockade of peripheral 5-HT3 receptors on extrinsic intestinal vagal and spinal afferent nerves
Stimulation of dopamine D2 receptors in the gastrointestinal tract
Activation of mu-opioid receptors to increase transit time
questions.explanation: While they have central actions, 5-HT3 antagonists exert their primary antiemetic effect by inhibiting peripheral 5-HT3 receptors on intestinal vagal and spinal afferents.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What potential risk is associated with long-term use of Magnesium-containing osmotic laxatives in patients with renal insufficiency?
options: Severe hypermagnesemia due to impaired renal excretion
questions.explanation: Magnesium is excreted by the kidneys; renal insufficiency can cause dangerous systemic accumulation resulting in hypermagnesemia.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What safety finding is highlighted regarding the use of a single dose of Dexamethasone (up to 8 mg) for preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV)?
options: It significantly increases postoperative wound infection rates and delays healing in diabetic patients
It does not increase the risk of postoperative wound or systemic infections, nor does it delay wound healing even in patients with diabetes mellitus
It causes immediate severe adrenal crisis within 2 hours of administration
It induces acute necrotizing pancreatitis in surgical patients
questions.explanation: Single doses of up to 8 mg of dexamethasone are safe and do not increase infection risk or impair wound healing, even in diabetics.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which antiemetic agent is a muscarinic receptor antagonist best tolerated as a transdermal patch for the prevention of motion sickness?
questions.explanation: Hyoscine is a muscarinic antagonist used for motion sickness that is better tolerated via transdermal patch to minimize systemic anticholinergic side effects.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which centrally and peripherally acting drug is an alpha-2 receptor agonist utilized to treat chronic diarrhea in diabetic patients and opioid withdrawal?
questions.explanation: Clonidine stimulates fluid/electrolyte absorption and inhibits secretion via alpha-2 agonism, helping diabetic diarrhea and opiate withdrawal diarrhea.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which dual central and peripheral dopamine (D2) receptor antagonist is widely utilized to enhance gastric emptying and increase lower esophageal sphincter (LES) pressure?
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide blocks central and peripheral D2 receptors, acting as an antiemetic and a prokinetic agent that increases LES pressure and gastric emptying.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which neurokinin-1 (NK1) receptor antagonist is formulated as an intravenous prodrug that is converted to aprepitant within 30 minutes following infusion?
questions.explanation: Fosaprepitant is an intravenous formulation administered as a 32 mg dose that rapidly converts to aprepitant in the body.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which severe neurological adverse effect profile is classically associated with prolonged or high-dose Metoclopramide therapy due to central dopamine blockade?
options: Peripheral sensory neuropathy and motor neuron disease
Extrapyramidal effects including dystonia, akathisia, and parkinsonian features
questions.explanation: Central dopamine blockade by metoclopramide frequently precipitates extrapyramidal symptoms such as dystonia and akathisia.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Why does Loperamide possess a favorable safety profile compared to other opioid agonists regarding addiction potential?
options: It is rapidly metabolized by gastric acid into an inactive peptide
It has poor central nervous system penetration and lacks analgesic properties
It selectively binds exclusively to colonic mucosal mu-receptors without touching neural tissue
It is completely insoluble in lipid membranes
questions.explanation: Loperamide exhibits poor CNS penetration, meaning it does not cause central opioid effects or addiction at therapeutic doses.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: According to the American College of Gastroenterology guidelines (2024) presented in the lecture, what is the duration and structure of first-line Quadruple Therapy for H. pylori eradication?
options: 7 days of a single PPI and Amoxicillin
14 days of a PPI (twice daily), Bismuth subsalicylate, Metronidazole, and Tetracycline (4 times daily), followed by PPI once daily for 4–6 weeks
21 days of continuous triple antibiotic therapy without acid suppression
3 days of high-dose intravenous pantoprazole alone
questions.explanation: First-line quadruple therapy runs for 14 days with PPI, bismuth, metronidazole, and tetracycline, followed by a PPI for 4–6 weeks.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Approximately what percentage of total 24-hour gastric acid secretion is inhibited by standard therapeutic doses of Proton Pump Inhibitors?
options: Exactly 100% with no basal acid remaining
questions.explanation: PPIs inhibit about 90–98% of 24-hour acid secretion, suppressing both fasting and meal-stimulated acid release.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How do Antacids chemically interact with hydrochloric acid in the stomach?
options: They act as biological enzymes that digest the acid molecules into amino acids.
They are alkaline compounds that react directly with HCl to neutralize its activity, raising gastric pH
They coat the vagus nerve to block cholinergic acid stimulation.
They inhibit the release of gastrin from G-cells in the antrum.
questions.explanation: Antacids are alkaline compounds that neutralize gastric hydrochloric acid through direct chemical reactions.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How do Histamine H_2 receptor antagonists (such as cimetidine and ranitidine) primarily reduce gastric acid secretion?
options: By directly destroying the parietal cell membrane
By competitively blocking histamine H_2 receptors on parietal cells, reducing cAMP-dependent acid secretion
By acting as irreversible agonists of inhibitory prostaglandin receptors
By binding directly to potassium channels in the gastric lumen
questions.explanation: H_2 blockers competitively inhibit histamine at parietal cell H_2 receptors, suppressing the cAMP pathway and acid output.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How do Proton Pump Inhibitors enhance the eradication of Helicobacter pylori when combined with antibiotic regimens?
options: By directly stimulating the immune system's neutrophil oxidative burst
By exhibiting direct antimicrobial activity and raising intragastric pH, which decreases the minimal therapeutic concentration of antibiotics required
By forming a physical barrier over the gastric mucosa that traps the bacteria
By chelating mucosal iron stores required for bacterial replication
questions.explanation: PPIs have direct antimicrobial effects and increase intragastric pH, lowering the MIC of antibiotics against H. pylori.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: In comparison to H_2 receptor antagonists, what is a primary clinical advantage of Proton Pump Inhibitors regarding ulcer healing times?
options: PPIs require twice as long to achieve symptom relief.
PPIs afford rapid symptom relief and faster healing of duodenal ulcers (within 4 weeks) and gastric ulcers (6–8 weeks)
PPIs work exclusively at night, whereas H_2 blockers work during the day.
PPIs have zero drug interactions compared to H_2 blockers.
questions.explanation: PPIs provide more rapid symptom relief and ulcer healing compared to H_2 blockers.
questions.topic: Pharmacology: acid suppression and ulcer healing
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Long-term or chronic use of Proton Pump Inhibitors can potentially increase the risk of which nutritional deficiency due to decreased gastric acid secretion?
options: Vitamin B12 deficiency, as well as impaired calcium and magnesium absorption
Essential amino acid wasting and protein-losing enteropathy
questions.explanation: HCl enhances vitamin B12 release and calcium/magnesium absorption; suppressing acid can lead to vitamin B12 deficiency, bone fractures, and hypomagnesemia.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What antibiotics comprise the alternative quadruple therapy regimen for H. pylori eradication mentioned in the lecture?
options: Clarithromycin, Amoxicillin, and Metronidazole (administered twice daily alongside a PPI for 14 days)
questions.explanation: The alternative regimen includes a PPI plus clarithromycin, amoxicillin, and metronidazole for 14 days.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What characteristic clinical syndrome can occur when high doses of Calcium Carbonate are ingested concurrently with calcium-rich foods?
options: Milk-alkali syndrome (characterized by hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, and alkalosis)
Fanconi syndrome and proximal tubular acidosis
questions.explanation: High doses of calcium carbonate with calcium-rich foods can result in milk-alkali syndrome.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is a well-documented endocrine side effect specifically associated with Cimetidine (an older H_2 blocker) due to its anti-androgenic properties?
options: Gynecomastia, galactorrhea, and impotence in men
questions.explanation: Cimetidine blocks androgen receptors and inhibits estradiol metabolism, leading to gynecomastia and impotence.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the clinical consequence of co-administering certain PPIs (such as omeprazole) with Clopidogrel?
options: Enhanced antiplatelet activation and increased bleeding risk
Inhibition of hepatic CYP2C19, which decreases the activation of clopidogrel and its antiplatelet activity, increasing thromboembolism risk
Immediate precipitation of severe neutropenia and bone marrow failure
Complete neutralization of the PPI's acid-suppressive capability
questions.explanation: Most PPIs inhibit CYP2C19, blocking the bioactivation of clopidogrel and elevating thromboembolic risks.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the mechanism of action of Sucralfate in the management of peptic ulcer disease?
options: It neutralizes hydrochloric acid in the gastric lumen within seconds.
In acidic pH, it forms a viscous sticky gel that binds selectively to ulcer craters for up to 6 hours and stimulates prostaglandin/bicarbonate secretion
It permanently blocks peripheral histamine H_2 receptors on parietal cells.
It eradicates Helicobacter pylori via direct bactericidal membrane disruption.
questions.explanation: Sucralfate creates a protective physical barrier by binding to ulcers in acidic environments and stimulates mucosal defenses.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the precise chemical and pharmacological nature of Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) upon administration?
options: Active hydrophilic quaternary amines that neutralize acid directly in the gastric lumen
Lipophilic weak bases administered as inactive prodrugs that concentrate in acidic canaliculi and bind covalently to the H^+/K^+-ATPase enzyme
Competitive, reversible antagonists of histamine H_2 receptors on parietal cells
Mucosal protective polymers that form a sticky gel in neutral pH environments
questions.explanation: PPIs are lipophilic weak bases, given as inactive prodrugs, which accumulate in acidic canaliculi and irreversibly bind the proton pump.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary clinical benefit of administering Proton Pump Inhibitors via a nasogastric tube in critically ill patients?
options: Prevention of bleeding from stress-related gastritis and mucosal ulceration
Eradication of hospital-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
Permanent acceleration of gastric emptying to prevent aspiration pneumonia
questions.explanation: Stress ulcer prophylaxis with PPIs significantly decreases the risk of stress-related mucosal bleeding in critically ill patients.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the recommended timing for administering oral Proton Pump Inhibitors relative to meals to achieve optimal bioavailability and efficacy?
options: Immediately after a high-fat meal to enhance lipid-based absorption
On an empty stomach, approximately 1 hour before a meal, because food decreases bioavailability by 50%
Exactly at bedtime regardless of meals to maximize nocturnal acid breakthrough
Divided evenly every 4 hours throughout the day
questions.explanation: Food decreases PPI bioavailability by about 50%, so they should be taken on an empty stomach 1 hour before a meal.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What rebound phenomenon may occur upon abrupt discontinuation of long-term Proton Pump Inhibitor therapy?
options: Rebound acid hypersecretion driven by hypergastrinemia
questions.explanation: Long-term acid suppression elevates gastrin production (hypergastrinemia), which can lead to rebound acid hypersecretion when stopping the drug.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which class of antacids is associated with the production of carbon dioxide gas (CO_2), leading to gastric distention, belching, and potential metabolic alkalosis?
questions.explanation: Both sodium bicarbonate and calcium carbonate react with HCl to produce CO_2, causing gastric distention, belching, and systemic metabolic alkalosis.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which pathological condition is characterized by massive gastric acid hypersecretion secondary to a gastrin-secreting tumor, which is successfully controlled by Proton Pump Inhibitors?
questions.explanation: Gastrinomas cause massive acid hypersecretion leading to severe ulceration, which is managed effectively by PPIs.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which physiological mechanism describes the protective role of Prostaglandins (PGE_2 and PGI_2) in the gastric mucosa?
options: Stimulation of parietal cell histamine release and cAMP-dependent acid secretion
Promotion of mucosal blood flow, enhancement of mucus and bicarbonate secretion, and inhibition of gastric acid secretion
Direct covalent binding and permanent inactivation of the H^+/K^+-ATPase proton pump
Neutralization of luminal hydrochloric acid via systemic systemic absorption
questions.explanation: Prostaglandins enhance mucosal defenses by promoting blood flow, stimulating mucus and bicarbonate secretion, and inhibiting acid secretion.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which specific Proton Pump Inhibitors are noted in the lecture as having no significant cytochrome P450 drug interactions, making them safer when co-prescribed with drugs like clopidogrel?
questions.explanation: Pantoprazole and rabeprazole lack significant drug interactions compared to omeprazole, esomeprazole, and lansoprazole.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which systemic antacid requires careful restriction or avoidance in patients with hypertension or heart failure due to its sodium content?
questions.explanation: Sodium bicarbonate is absorbed systemically and provides a sodium load that can exacerbate fluid retention in hypertension and heart failure.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Why are Magnesium Hydroxide and Aluminum Hydroxide commonly formulated and administered together in commercial antacid preparations (e.g., Maolox)?
options: To accelerate the systemic absorption of both cations into the bloodstream
To neutralize the individual bowel motility effects (magnesium causes osmotic diarrhea, while aluminum causes constipation)
To induce immediate release of carbon dioxide gas for rapid upper GI decompression
To prevent the hepatic metabolism of concurrent proton pump inhibitors
questions.explanation: Magnesium salts cause diarrhea and aluminum salts cause constipation; combining them balances bowel function.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Why must oral formulations of Proton Pump Inhibitors be designed with delayed-release enteric coatings?
options: To prevent immediate systemic absorption in the oral cavity and esophagus
To protect the acid-labile prodrug from premature degradation in the acidic gastric juice before reaching the alkaline intestinal lumen for absorption
To ensure the drug binds to mucosal prostaglandins rather than parietal cells
To eliminate hepatic first-pass metabolism entirely
questions.explanation: PPIs are acid-labile and require enteric coatings to prevent gastric acid degradation before absorption in the intestine.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the immediate pharmacological treatment used to stabilize cardiac membranes in severe hyperkalemia?
options: Intravenous calcium gluconate (e.g., 30 mL of 10% solution)
Loop diuretic monotherapy without fluid support
questions.explanation: IV calcium gluconate stabilizes cardiac cell membranes against electrical instability and arrhythmias during hyperkalemic emergencies.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary mechanism of action of Tranexamic acid (TXA) when administered for surgical hemorrhage?
options: Direct stimulation of platelet aggregation receptors.
Inhibition of fibrinolysis by blocking plasminogen activation.
questions.explanation: TXA is an antifibrinolytic agent that prevents blood clot breakdown by competitively blocking plasminogen activation.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: A 58‑year‑old man with a history of chronic pancreatitis presents with a sudden, severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and a markedly elevated serum amylase. An abdominal CT scan confirms a necrotizing pancreatitis with a fluid collection. Which of the following pharmacologic agents is most appropriate to reduce the risk of infection in the necrotic collection while also decreasing the systemic inflammatory response?
questions.explanation: Cefepime, a fourth‑generation cephalosporin, provides broad coverage against gram‑negative rods, gram‑positive cocci and anaerobes, which are the most common organisms in infected pancreatic necrosis. It also has a favorable pharmacokinetic profile for penetration into necrotic tissue. Cefazolin and cefotaxime lack adequate anaerobic coverage, while metronidazole alone does not cover gram‑negative organisms. Thus cefepime is the most appropriate choice to reduce infection risk and dampen systemic inflammation.
questions.source: Principles of antimicrobial therapy in necrotizing pancreatitis
questions.topic: Principles of antimicrobial therapy in necrotizing pancreatitis
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Corticosteroid Therapy Under what clinical circumstance are intravenous corticosteroids (e.g., hydrocortisone 200\text{ mg/day}) specifically indicated in the management of septic shock?
options: Routinely in all patients immediately upon presentation to prevent mild fever
Only when blood pressure is refractory to fluid resuscitation and moderate-to-high dose vasopressor therapy
To treat concurrent chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbations
As a prophylactic measure to prevent stress-induced hyperglycemia
questions.explanation: Corticosteroids are not recommended for routine use in sepsis but are indicated when hemodynamic stability remains refractory to fluid resuscitation and vasopressors, as relative adrenal insufficiency may be present.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: First-Line Vasopressor Selection If fluid resuscitation fails to restore an adequate blood pressure in septic shock, which vasoactive agent is recommended as the first-line vasopressor of choice?
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine provides potent alpha-1-mediated vasoconstriction with modest beta-1 inotropic support, making it superior and safer than dopamine or phenylephrine for restoring vascular tone in septic shock.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: If fluid resuscitation fails to restore adequate blood pressure in septic shock, which first-line vasopressor is standardly initiated?
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine provides potent alpha-1 vasoconstriction with minimal chronotropy, making it the vasopressor of choice to restore MAP in septic shock.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Second-Line Vasopressor Additions If a patient with septic shock requires escalating doses of norepinephrine to maintain target MAP, which adjunctive vasoactive agent is most commonly added next to exploit alternative receptor pathways (V1 receptors)?
options: Vasopressin (at a fixed dose of 0.03 units/min)
questions.explanation: Vasopressin acts on vascular V1 receptors independent of adrenergic pathways and is standardly added as a fixed-dose infusion (0.03 units/min) to reduce norepinephrine requirements and treat relative vasopressin deficiency.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: A 65‑year‑old patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is admitted for an acute exacerbation and is started on intravenous methylprednisolone. Which of the following is the most likely adverse effect of prolonged high‑dose steroid therapy in this patient?
questions.explanation: High‑dose systemic steroids cause gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance, leading to hyperglycaemia. Hypocalcaemia, hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia are not typical adverse effects of steroids.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: In the medical management of Hydatid cyst disease, which antihelmintic medication is administered long-term (e.g., for months)?
questions.explanation: Benzimidazoles like albendazole (10–15 mg/kg in two daily doses) are given for months (with or without praziquantel) to medicalize cysts, reduce viability, and prevent recurrence perioperatively.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary drug of choice for treating Fasciola Hepatica (Sheep liver fluke) infection?
questions.explanation: Triclabendazole is the specific and highly effective medical treatment of choice for fascioliasis in humans.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the standard anti-amoebic drug used to treat invasive intestinal amoebiasis and amoebic liver abscess?
options: Metronidazole (or Tinidazole), followed by a luminal amoebicide like diloxanide furoate
questions.explanation: Tissue-invasive amoebiasis is treated with nitroimidazoles like metronidazole or tinidazole to eliminate invasive trophozoites, followed by a luminal agent to clear cysts.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the WHO guideline recommendation regarding prolonged postoperative antibiotic prophylaxis?
options: Continue antibiotics for at least 14 days post-op to prevent all infections.
Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis administration should not be prolonged after completion of the operation.
Stop antibiotics only when stitches are removed.
Double the dose post-op if the surgery lasted over 1 hour.
questions.explanation: Prolonged postoperative antibiotic prophylaxis provides no additional benefit and fosters bacterial resistance; WHO guidelines state prophylaxis should not be extended past the completion of the procedure.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: When should Surgical Antibiotic Prophylaxis (SAP) ideally be administered?
options: Within 20 minutes before surgical incision, taking into account the antibiotic's half-life.
Immediately after wound closure in the recovery room.
Only if the patient develops a fever on postoperative day 3.
questions.explanation: Prophylactic antibiotics must be present in tissue at peak levels when the incision is made, requiring administration within 20 minutes prior to incision.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs) include direct factor Xa inhibitors and direct thrombin inhibitors. Which of the following is a direct thrombin inhibitor?
questions.explanation: Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor, whereas rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban are direct factor Xa inhibitors.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: In aspirin (salicylate) toxicity, patients frequently present with a complex mixed acid-base disturbance. What is the typical combination?
options: Primary respiratory alkalosis (direct stimulation of the respiratory center) combined with high anion gap metabolic acidosis (salicylate uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation)
Pure metabolic alkalosis and respiratory alkalosis
Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis alone
questions.explanation: Salicylate overdose stimulates the brainstem respiratory center (causing respiratory alkalosis) while simultaneously disrupting cellular metabolism to generate organic acids (causing HAGMA).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the immediate life-threatening risk associated with extremely rapid correction of chronic severe metabolic acidosis using sodium bicarbonate?
options: Severe hypokalemia, paradoxical intracellular acidosis (as CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier faster than HCO3-), and volume overload
questions.explanation: Rapid bicarbonate administration can cause overshoot alkalosis, hypokalemia, ionized hypocalcemia, and worsening intracellular acidosis because CO2 diffuses across cell membranes faster than charged bicarbonate.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the specific monoclonal antibody fragment used as the reversal agent for the direct thrombin inhibitor dabigatran?
questions.explanation: Idarucizumab is a specific reversal agent that binds directly to dabigatran to neutralize its anticoagulant effect. Part 2: Acid-Base Disturbances (Q26–Q50)
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the specific pharmacological reversal agent for Warfarin in cases of severe bleeding or emergency surgery?
options: Vitamin K (phytomenadione) and Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC)
questions.explanation: Vitamin K replenishes clotting factors, while PCC provides rapid reversal of vitamin K antagonists in life-threatening bleeding.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What life-threatening complication of unfractionated heparin therapy is characterized by a paradoxical drop in platelet count coupled with new or worsening thrombosis?
questions.explanation: HIT is an immune-mediated adverse reaction to heparin-platelet factor 4 complexes causing thrombosis and thrombocytopenia.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What specific blood test monitoring is required when administering therapeutic doses of intravenous Unfractionated Heparin (UFH)?
questions.explanation: UFH requires regular monitoring of APTT to maintain the therapeutic anticoagulation range (typically 1.5 to 2.5 times control).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: When initiating treatment with certain DOACs like dabigatran or edoxaban for acute VTE, what is required prior to starting the oral agent?
options: Initial parenteral overlap/cover with Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH) for at least 5 days
Insertion of an inferior vena cava filter
questions.explanation: Dabigatran and edoxaban require initial parenteral anticoagulation (LMWH or fondaparinux) for at least 5 days before transitioning to the oral drug.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which of the following represents a primary contraindication to pharmacological VTE prophylaxis (such as LMWH or unfractionated heparin)?
options: Active bleeding or high risk of major hemorrhage (e.g., recent hemorrhagic stroke or active GI bleed)
questions.explanation: Anticoagulation is contraindicated in patients with active bleeding or severe hemorrhagic diathesis.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Why is Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH) generally preferred over Unfractionated Heparin (UFH) for outpatient or standard inpatient VTE treatment?
options: It requires routine daily monitoring of APTT.
It has a more predictable pharmacokinetic profile, higher bioavailability, and does not routinely require laboratory monitoring of APTT.
It is completely reversible without any antidotes.
It can only be administered orally.
questions.explanation: LMWH provides predictable dose-response characteristics and subcutaneous administration convenience without routine coagulation monitoring.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most important principle to prevent postoperative wound infection?
options: A. Use of prophylactic antibiotics before incision
B. Strict aseptic technique during surgery
D. Early mobilization of the patient
questions.explanation: Strict aseptic technique during surgery (option B) is the cornerstone of preventing wound infection, as it eliminates contamination at the source. While prophylactic antibiotics (option A) are helpful, they cannot replace proper asepsis. Immediate dressing (option C) and early mobilization (option D) are supportive measures but not primary preventive strategies.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Following a suspected transfusion reaction, what vital administrative step must be performed with the used blood unit?
options: Dispose of it immediately to prevent accidental re-infusion.
Send it back to the blood bank team along with a clerical check of patient ID and product info.
Autoclave the unit in the operating theatre.
Record the serial number and empty the contents down the sink.
questions.explanation: The used unit must not be discarded; it must be referred back to the blood bank along with clerical verification to investigate potential mix-ups.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How is a massive blood transfusion clinically defined?
options: Transfusing more than 2 units in 12 hours
Replacing a patient's whole blood volume within 24 hours, or transfusing > 4 units in 1 hour or 50% of blood volume in 3 hours
Any transfusion exceeding 10 units over a 7-day hospital admission
Transfusing whole blood exclusively within the operating room
questions.explanation: Massive transfusion criteria include replacing whole blood volume within 24 hours, or giving > 4 units in 1 hour or 50% of blood volume in 3 hours.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Under what recommended storage conditions can Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) be kept for up to 1 year?
options: Incubated at room temperature with constant agitation
Kept in an ultra-cold freezer at -80^\circ\text{C} for 5 years
questions.explanation: Plasma (FFP) is stored frozen at -18^\circ\text{C} or colder, with a shelf life of up to 1 year.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are blood substitutes (artificial blood) primarily designed to achieve?
options: Provide permanent cellular immunity against bacterial sepsis.
Mimic biological blood functions by restoring volume and carrying oxygen.
Permanently replace bone marrow stem cell niches.
Eliminate the need for ABO typing in all surgical emergencies.
questions.explanation: Blood substitutes (such as hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers and perfluorocarbon emulsions) are developed to mimic blood functions like volume restoration and oxygen transport.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What immediate action must be taken first when a transfusion reaction is suspected during a blood administration?
options: Administer high-flow oxygen and intravenous adrenaline immediately.
Stop or pause the transfusion while keeping the IV line open with 0.9% normal saline.
Discard the transfusion bag and tubing directly into biohazard waste.
Increase the infusion rate to flush the remaining volume.
questions.explanation: The immediate step is to stop or pause the transfusion and maintain IV access with normal saline for supportive care.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is generally accepted as the trigger hemoglobin threshold for blood transfusion in stable surgical patients?
options: When hemoglobin drops below 7\text{ g/dL} (agreed threshold)
questions.explanation: The agreed transfusion threshold for anemia in surgical patients is when hemoglobin falls below 7\text{ g/dL}.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the most commonly encountered non-infectious complication of blood transfusion in clinical practice?
options: Febrile non-hemolytic reaction (characterized by mild fever and chills)
questions.explanation: Febrile non-hemolytic reactions (presenting with mild fever and chills) are the most frequent transfusion reactions encountered.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary cause of hypocalcemia and myocardial suppression during rapid massive blood transfusions?
questions.explanation: Anticoagulant preservatives contain citrate, which binds to ionized calcium and can cause citrate toxicity leading to hypocalcemia.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary physiological driver and oxygen-sensing mechanism for blood cell synthesis in the bone marrow?
options: Hepatic thrombopoietin secretion triggered by systemic alkalosis.
Renal hypoxia triggering secretion of the hormone erythropoietin (EPO).
Splenic macrophage destruction of senescent erythrocytes.
questions.explanation: Oxygen sensing in the kidney under hypoxic conditions stimulates the release of erythropoietin (EPO), which binds to bone marrow progenitor cells to promote red blood cell production.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the recommended storage temperature and shelf life for platelets?
options: Room temperature (20\text{--}24^\circ\text{C}) with constant agitation for 5 to 7 days
Stored in an ice bath for 48 hours
questions.explanation: Platelets are stored at room temperature (20\text{--}24^\circ\text{C}) with constant agitation for 5 to 7 days (making bacterial contamination a notable risk).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the standard shelf life and storage temperature for packed red blood cells stored with preservative solutions?
questions.explanation: Packed red blood cells can be stored refrigerated at 1\text{--}6^\circ\text{C} for 35 to 42 days depending on the preservative solution used.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What specific coagulation factors and proteins are contained in Cryoprecipitate?
options: Factor VIII, fibrinogen, and von Willebrand factor
Prothrombin and Factors VII, IX, and X
questions.explanation: Cryoprecipitate supplies concentrated Factor VIII, fibrinogen, and von Willebrand factor for specific bleeding risks and deficiencies.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which blood component is primarily indicated for treating patients with severe thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction in cases of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)?
questions.explanation: Platelets are used to treat thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction associated with conditions like DIC.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which metabolic complication is most characteristically associated with massive blood transfusion due to the breakdown and leakage from stored red blood cells?
questions.explanation: Potassium leaks out of stored red blood cells over time, predisposing patients to hyperkalemia during massive transfusions.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions is an indication for administering Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP)?
options: Liver disease, severe burns, and DIC
questions.explanation: FFP contains plasma proteins, clotting factors, and antibodies used to treat clotting disorders, liver disease, severe burns, and DIC.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Within what time window during blood administration should a patient be monitored most closely for signs of an acute reaction?
options: Only after the entire unit has been completely infused
questions.explanation: Close monitoring is vital especially during the first 15 minutes of transfusion, when acute life-threatening reactions typically manifest.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How does Apoptosis fundamentally differ from Necrosis regarding energy requirement, plasma membrane integrity, and surrounding tissue response?
options: Apoptosis is energy-independent, causes plasma membrane breakdown, and triggers severe inflammation 1
Apoptosis is an active, energy-dependent (ATP-requiring) process where the plasma membrane remains intact, forming apoptotic bodies that are phagocytosed without inciting an inflammatory response 1
Necrosis requires active gene transcription and preserves cellular organelles
Both pathways result in widespread tissue scar formation 1
questions.explanation: Apoptosis is an organized, ATP-dependent programmed death pathway. The plasma membrane remains intact, blebbing into apoptotic bodies that are cleared by macrophages without provoking an inflammatory response or leaving a scar 1 . Necrosis is passive, uncontrolled, ruptures membranes, and triggers acute inflammation 1 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Rupture of lysosomal membranes during severe, irreversible cell injury leads to which pathological event?
options: Release of hydrolytic enzymes (RNases, DNases, proteases) into the cytosol causing cellular autodigestion 1
Immediate activation of the extrinsic Fas death receptor
questions.explanation: Lysosomal membrane breach releases active acid hydrolases (RNases, DNases, proteases) into the cytoplasm, resulting in enzymatic digestion of cellular components (autodigestion) 1 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Sustained influx of calcium ( C a 2 + ) into the cytosol during ischemic or toxic injury damages cells by activating which set of intracellular enzymes?
questions.explanation: High cytosolic calcium activates phospholipases (degrade cell membranes), proteases (break down cytoskeletal/membrane proteins), endonucleases (fragment DNA), and ATPases (accelerate ATP depletion) 1 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are the primary clinical and pathological differences between Dry Gangrene and Wet Gangrene?
options: Dry gangrene involves bacterial superinfection, whereas wet gangrene is sterile

Dry gangrene is caused by ischemia alone (mummified, dry, black with a clear demarcation line); Wet gangrene involves ischemia with bacterial superinfection (swollen, foul-smelling, lacking demarcation line, carrying high sepsis risk) 1
Dry gangrene requires emergency surgery, whereas wet gangrene can be managed expectantly 1
Wet gangrene occurs exclusively in the brain, while dry gangrene occurs in internal viscera
questions.explanation: Dry gangrene results from pure arterial ischemia without significant infection, forming dry, black, mummified tissue with a clear line of demarcation 1 . Wet gangrene features secondary bacterial superinfection, producing swollen, foul-smelling tissue without a clear demarcation line, requiring urgent surgical intervention due to high sepsis risk 1 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are the primary molecular targets of Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) during oxidative stress in injured cells?
options: Lipid peroxidation of membranes, protein cross-linking/fragmentation, and DNA strand breaks 1
Active glycogen synthesis and cell wall thickening
questions.explanation: Free radicals contain unpaired electrons that react with lipids (causing membrane peroxidation), proteins (causing cross-linking and fragmentation), and nucleic acids (causing single/double strand DNA breaks) 1 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What biochemical process accounts for the chalky white deposits observed grossly in Fat Necrosis associated with acute pancreatitis?
options: Saponification, where free fatty acids liberated by active lipases combine with calcium 1
questions.explanation: In acute pancreatitis, leaked activated pancreatic lipases digest peripancreatic adipose tissue. The liberated free fatty acids bind calcium ions to form insoluble chalky white soap deposits (saponification) 1 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What defines Fatty Change (Steatosis), and in which organ is it most commonly encountered following hypoxic, toxic, or metabolic injury?
options: Accumulation of triglyceride vacuoles within the cytoplasm, observed predominantly in the liver 1
Deposition of lipofuscin in cardiac myocytes 1
questions.explanation: Steatosis is the abnormal accumulation of triglyceride lipid vacuoles within parenchyma cells, occurring most commonly in the liver as a response to alcohol, toxins, obesity, diabetes, or hypoxia 1 .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What gross and microscopic features define Caseous Necrosis, and what is its classic etiology?
options: Bright pink amorphous vessel wall deposits seen in vasculitis 1
